newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair calls for sleaze probe as row widens.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair calls for sleaze probe as row widens.

text.p: British opposition leader Tony Blair called on Wednesday for an independent investigation into political donations as a row over parliamentary corruption in the ruling Conservative party widened.
A former Conservative minister admitted on Tuesday he took money from a parliamentary lobbyist, but said he did not believe he had entered into any financial arrangement as a result.
The Guardian newspaper published a list of 24 members of parliament from all three major parties who had received donations to their fighting funds from the same lobbyist.

It was not suggested the MPs had done anything illegal in accepting the donations of up to 5,000 pounds ($7,500) but taking funds from a lobbyist inevitably led to questions about the possible purchase of influence.
The former minister, Neil Hamilton, sparked a major furore when he pulled out of a libel case against the Guardian on Monday, only hours before it was due to start.

Hamilton was forced to resign as trade minister in October 1994 after the Guardian accused him of accepting money from Mohammed al-Fayed, the Egyptian-born owner of London's luxury Harrods store, in return for tabling questions in parliament.
Hamilton continues to deny the newspaper's claims that he had accepted cash in exchange for asking questions in parliament and said he stopped the libel case because of lack of funds.

But Hamilton told a BBC television interviewer he had accepted two payments totalling 10,000 pounds from parliamentary lobbyist Ian Greer in the late 1980s. The payments were made in exchange for introducing a client to the lobbyist, he said.
In October 1994, Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine had received an assurance from Hamilton that he did not have a financial arrangement with Greer.
Labour leader Blair said it was now important for the reputation of parliament that the whole area of political funding be examined.
"It would be wrong and I think unfortunate if people thought that all members of parliament were taking cash for questions," the Labour leader told a BBC television interviewer.
Stressing the need for transparency, he said funding should be investigated by leading judge Lord Nolan, who has recently chaired a commission into standards in public life.
Asked about two Labour MPs who has accepted donation from Greer, Blair said that accepting political donations was "completely different" from asking parliamentary questions in return for cash.
Prime Minister John Major and Heseltine had both been subpoenaed to testify in the Hamilton libel case.

Sixteen Conservative members of parliament have been forced to resign from government posts since 1992 because of sleaze allegations. Greer had also planned to sue the Guardian for libel, but he pulled out of the trial along with Hamilton.

The timing of the reports is particularly unwelcome for the Conservative Party because it is due next week to hold its last annual conference before the next general election. It lags Labour by more than 20 points in opinion polls.
